title: Redis Use Cases
summary: One in-memory engine, many jobs: pick the right data structure for caching, sessions, rate limits, locks, leaderboards, queues and geo, and know where Redis' durability ends.

blocks.text: Framing: design the shared Redis platform for a large e-commerce app that serves product caching, user sessions, API rate limiting, flash-sale inventory locks, a gamified leaderboard, delayed jobs and a 'stores near me' feature.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: At 1.5M ops/s and ~100k per node I'd want about 20 primaries with one replica each, and I'd split use cases with different durability needs into separate clusters.

Cache:        GET p:42 / SETEX p:42 300 <json>
Session:      HSET sess:<id> uid 42 cart 3 ; EXPIRE sess:<id> 1800
Rate limit:   EVAL token_bucket.lua 1 rl:{key} cap rate now
Lock:         SET lock:sku42 <uuid> NX PX 5000 ; release via Lua compare-and-delete
Inventory:    DECRBY stock:sku42 1  (reject if result < 0, then INCRBY back)
Leaderboard:  ZINCRBY lb:week 10 u42 ; ZREVRANGE lb:week 0 99 WITHSCORES ; ZREVRANK lb:week u42
Delayed job:  ZADD jobs <runAt> <jobId> ; Lua: ZRANGEBYSCORE jobs 0 now LIMIT 0 50 + ZREM
Stream queue: XADD orders * id 9 ; XREADGROUP GROUP g c1 COUNT 10 STREAMS orders > ; XACK
Geo:          GEOADD stores 73.85 18.52 pune-1 ; GEOSEARCH stores FROMLONLAT .. BYRADIUS 5 km
Uniques:      PFADD uv:2026-10-29 u42 ; PFCOUNT uv:2026-10-29

blocks.caption: Separate clusters by durability and blast radius

items: Cache cluster may evict anything; state cluster (sessions, jobs, rate limits) uses `noeviction` + AOF.
Keeping them apart stops a cache stampede from evicting sessions or jobs.
16,384 hash slots; slot = CRC16(key) mod 16384; each primary owns a range.
Clients cache the slot map; a `MOVED` reply updates it, `ASK` handles keys mid-migration.
Multi-key commands and Lua need all keys in one slot: use hash tags `{user:42}:cart`.
Failover: replicas detect primary failure by gossip, a majority of primaries vote, a replica is promoted (seconds).
Replication is async: acknowledged writes can be lost on failover. `WAIT 1 100` narrows but doesn't close the gap.

blocks.title: Trap
blocks.text: Hash tags concentrate keys: tagging everything with `{tenant}` puts a big tenant on one slot and one node.

cols.title: Atomic counter (DECRBY)
cons: Redis is not the ledger; must reconcile with DB

cols.title: Distributed lock per SKU
cons: Serializes all buyers of a hot SKU

blocks.text: Pattern: preload `stock:sku42 = 1000`. Each buy runs a Lua script: if stock > 0, decrement and push an order event to a Stream; else reject. A consumer writes orders to the DB transactionally. Nightly reconciliation compares Redis vs DB.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: For a flash sale I'd avoid locks: an atomic Lua decrement admits exactly N buyers in memory, and the database remains the ledger via an async order stream.

sections.title: Deep dive: persistence and when not to use Redis

blocks.title: Rule
blocks.text: Don't keep money, orders or anything you can't rebuild only in Redis. Use it in front of a durable store.

rows: Blocks the single thread, latency spikes
Split into buckets; `UNLINK` for async delete; scan for big keys
Client-side cache (Redis 6 tracking), replicas for reads, key sharding
Slow commands (KEYS, SMEMBERS on huge set)
Disable KEYS, use SCAN, slowlog alerts
Idempotent jobs, Streams with re-delivery, WAIT for critical writes

items.q: Why is Redis fast despite being single-threaded?
items.a: Everything is in memory, commands are tiny, it uses an event loop with epoll and no locks; since 6.0 network I/O can use threads while execution stays single-threaded.
Debated. It assumes bounded clock drift and pauses. Fine for efficiency; for correctness add fencing tokens or use a consensus system.

items.q: How would you implement a rate limiter shared across 50 gateways?
items.a: Token bucket or sliding window in a Lua script on Redis, key per client, fail-open on Redis outage with local fallback limits.
Streams are simple and fast but memory-bound with limited retention; Kafka is disk-based with long retention, partitions and high throughput.

items.q: How do you rebuild a leaderboard after data loss?
items.a: Replay scores from the DB or the event log into a new key, then RENAME atomically.
Ops/s, p99 latency, memory used vs maxmemory, evictions, keyspace hit ratio, replication lag, slowlog.

items: Single-threaded execution → every command is atomic.
Sorted set = leaderboards, sliding windows, delayed jobs.
16,384 slots; hash tags keep multi-key ops in one slot.
Async replication → failover can lose acked writes.
Lock release must compare the token (Lua).
Never the system of record for money.
